# Introduction

## The reversal of educational difference


Women born just after the Second World War were less likely than men of the same cohort to hold a degree. For every subsequent cohort, the gap has narrowed and reversed across most European countries, including Austria.

::: {#fig-tertiary-difference}
{{< include build/figures/tertiary_difference.qmd >}}
**The female educational advantage by cohort.**\
The measure and most of the design follow Erát [@erat2021], but the data include more countries (30) and survey rounds.\
*Source:* own calculations based on the rounds 1-11 of the European Social Survey[@europeansocialsurveyeuropeanresearchinfrastructureesseric2023; @europeansocialsurveyeuropeanresearchinfrastructureesseric2012; @europeansocialsurveyeuropeanresearchinfrastructureesseric2018; @europeansocialsurveyeuropeanresearchinfrastructureesseric2023a; @europeansocialsurveyeuropeanresearchinfrastructureesseric2025; @europeansocialsurveyeuropeanresearchinfrastructureesseric2025a; @europeansocialsurveyeuropeanresearchinfrastructureesseric2023b; @europeansocialsurveyeuropeanresearchinfrastructureesseric2023c; @europeansocialsurveyeuropeanresearchinfrastructureesseric2026; @europeansocialsurveyeuropeanresearchinfrastructureesseric2025b; @europeansocialsurveyeuropeanresearchinfrastructureesseric2026a].

:::

The reversal in @fig-tertiary-difference is an aggregation of individuals by sex, women's degree share in each cohort against men's. Individuals, however, pair, and a change in the education propagates into the educational composition of the couples. Education is both a strong social signal and a stratifying force [@kalmijn1998]. Consequently, how couples form is rarely random.

Educational assortative mating describes the non-random pattern of individuals selecting partners based on education level^[There are two types of assortative mating: positive and negative (also called disassortative), in which partners are similar and dissimilar to each other, respectively. In this thesis, for brevity, assortative mating means the positive kind.]. The sorting's consequences extend beyond the couples themselves, from the socioeconomic status of the household to the life chances of their children. Between households, sorting on education is responsible for a significant share of cross-sectional income inequality^[Nevertheless, changes in sorting over time were not associated with the changes in household income inequality.] [@eika2019]. Within the household, both genders were shown to have lower well-being when man is more educated in the partnership [@wang2025]. Across generations, sorting both reinforces educational reproduction, as resources are concentrated on the children of educated parents, and reduces it since those parents tend to have fewer children [@wittemann2024].
